one_liner: Julia NUFFT library for CPU, CUDA and AMD GPUs; its shared-memory GPU spreading beats cuFINUFFT on dense 3D type-1 transforms.
what_it_does: Computes type-1 (non-uniform to uniform) and type-2 (uniform to non-uniform) non-uniform FFTs in 1, 2 and 3 dimensions for real or complex non-uniform data. You build a PlanNUFFT(T, Ns; m, σ, backend), call set_points!, then exec_type1! or exec_type2!; passing backend = CUDABackend() or ROCBackend() runs the same code on a GPU. It also implements the AbstractNFFTs.jl interface (plan_nfft, mul!, adjoint), so it can stand in for NFFT.jl, but it is not a drop-in for FINUFFT's makeplan/setpts/exec API.
how_it_is_fast: It is the standard gridding NUFFT: spread each point onto an oversampled grid with a compact (backwards) Kaiser-Bessel kernel, run FFTW or cuFFT, then deconvolve; type 2 runs the steps in reverse. On the CPU, points are partitioned into spatial blocks for multithreading, and kernel weights use a piecewise FastApproximation. On the GPU there are two methods. The default :global_memory method sorts points into blocks and adds atomically into global memory. The :shared_memory method stages each grid block in workgroup shared memory and processes points in batches so that no shared-memory atomics are needed; the docs credit this for the gains over cuFINUFFT's SM method, which is based on Shih et al. 2021. Real-valued data use r2c/c2r FFTs and spread half as much data.
when_to_use: Dense 3D type-1 NUFFTs on NVIDIA GPUs (about one or more points per grid cell) with gpu_method = :shared_memory: on an H100 at 256^3 and tol 1e-6 it ran 2.7-4.3x faster than cuFINUFFT's best method (0.300 s vs 0.822 s at 168M points).
Real-valued non-uniform data such as particle densities or vortex filaments, where the r2c/c2r path halves spreading and FFT work; FINUFFT has no such path.
Julia codes that want one NUFFT implementation for CPU threads, CUDA and AMD GPUs, or that need callbacks to modify input and output on the fly.
Memory-constrained 3D GPU jobs: with σ = 1.5 the oversampled 256^3 grid is 384^3 (about 0.9 GB of ComplexF64) against cuFINUFFT's 512^3 (about 2.1 GB) at its default upsampfac of 2.0.
when_not_to_use: 2D (and probably 1D) GPU transforms. Open issue #69 shows it up to 11.5x slower than cuFINUFFT on a 128x128 grid (shared memory at 163,840 points: 0.0202 s vs 0.00175 s); the maintainer says the package is 'mostly optimised for 3D'.

Type-2 (interpolation) at high point density on the GPU, where it is 1.3-2.0x slower than cuFINUFFT with either method; type-1 with the default :global_memory method is about 1.5x slower at densities of 1 and above.
CPU-only work where FINUFFT is already available: the H100-node CPU rows range from about 1.9x faster to 1.8x slower depending on density and on the use_atomics setting.
AMD GPUs with many points on the default method: the docs say :global_memory 'scales very poorly' there, so switch to :shared_memory.
C, C++, Python or MATLAB callers: it needs a Julia runtime, while FINUFFT ships native interfaces for all of these.

integration.dependencies: Julia packages FFTW, KernelAbstractions, AcceleratedKernels, OhMyThreads, Atomix, Bessels, StaticArrays, AbstractFFTs, AbstractNFFTs, Adapt, TimerOutputs; package extensions for CUDA (CUDACore.jl v6 + cuFFT.jl v6), AMDGPU.jl (v1.0.5 or v2) and StructArrays
integration.min_toolchain: Julia 1.10 (Project.toml compat); the CUDA extension requires the CUDA.jl v6 package split (since v0.9.2)
integration.platforms: CPU on any Julia platform (multithreaded), NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA.jl, AMD GPUs through AMDGPU.jl; other KernelAbstractions backends in principle
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the plan holds point and buffer state that set_points! and exec_* overwrite, and multithreading happens inside each call (Julia threads on CPU)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — implements the AbstractNFFTs.jl (NFFT.jl-style) interface for complex data only, not FINUFFT's or FINUFFT.jl's makeplan/setpts/exec API; mode ordering and the kernel and σ parameters differ

gotchas: Harness parameter asymmetry explains most of the GPU result. The script fixes σ = 1.5 with HalfSupport(4), a width-8 kernel on a 384^3 grid, but never sets upsampfac for cuFINUFFT. cufinufft's auto choice (include/cufinufft/impl.h, v2.4.1) gives 2.0 for types 1 and 2, so ns = ceil(-log10(tol/10)) = 7 on a 512^3 grid. NonuniformFFTs therefore does a 2.37x smaller FFT but 1.49x more kernel evaluations per point (512 vs 343). Its low-density wins (1.66x type 1, 1.92x type 2 at 1,678 points) and its default-method losses at high density (1.53-1.55x on type 1) track those two ratios. cuFINUFFT has supported upsampfac = 1.25 on GPU since v2.3, and the script did not try it. Only the shared-memory type-1 rows win despite doing more kernel work per point.

On the CPU the two libraries also run different accuracy and work settings. FINUFFT 2.4.1 auto-picks upsampfac from heuristics.hpp with the density hard-coded to 1 (finufft_core.cpp), which gives 1.25 here at 24 threads and tol 1e-6. That means ns = 10 (1000 kernel evaluations per point vs 512) on a 320^3 grid, and FINUFFT's measured type-1 error is 3.73e-6, missing the requested 1e-6, against 1.28e-6 for NonuniformFFTs. Separately, the benchmark's σ = 1.5 is not the package default: PlanNUFFT defaults to σ = 2.0, which gives a 512^3 grid with a width-8 kernel, so an untuned plan will not reproduce the published curves.

The docs say the points are uniform in [0, 2π)^3, but run_benchmarks.jl draws standard-normal coordinates (randn with Xoshiro(42)) for both libraries. The cloud is clustered around the origin corner of the periodic box, which changes atomic contention during spreading, so results for genuinely uniform points may differ (not measured). Both libraries receive identical points and agree on accuracy to within about 25% on the GPU (type-1 error 1.74e-6 vs 1.39e-6).

Open bug #95 (2026-10-07): on the GPU, Float32 points slightly below 0 fold to exactly 2π and index one past the grid, which gives intermittent wrong results or CUDA illegal-memory-access errors. The CPU path is not affected; the workaround is to fold points into [0, 2π) yourself. v0.9.5 fixed a related out-of-bounds bug for points near L on certain grid sizes, and the benchmarked v0.8.3 predates that fix. The README GPU example also passes an undefined xp to set_points! (it should pass points).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The catalogued siblings in runtime-jit-beats-aot are language-runtime microbenchmarks (.NET JIT, Bun, ClangJIT) rather than libraries; the realistic alternative is the listed baseline FINUFFT/cuFINUFFT. Pick NonuniformFFTs.jl over it for dense 3D type-1 GPU work with the shared-memory method, or for real-valued data in Julia. Stay with FINUFFT for 2D GPU, high-density type 2, CPU-only work or non-Julia callers.
verified_claims_summary: The author benchmarked NonuniformFFTs.jl v0.8.3 (σ = 1.5, width-8 KB kernel) against FINUFFT v2.4.1 (nvc++ Release) and cuFINUFFT (nvcc from CUDA 12.8, sm_90) called through FINUFFT.jl v3.4.0, on one Jean Zay node share (2x Xeon Platinum 8468 with 24 cores used, one H100 80 GB), for 3D 256^3 ComplexF64 transforms at tol 1e-6. Times are BenchmarkTools medians of set_points plus exec. The GPU type-1 shared-memory method was 2.7-4.3x faster than cuFINUFFT's best at densities of 1-10, while the default method was 1.5x slower there and type 2 was slower at high density; CPU results were within about 2x either way, and the Julia version is not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained by a single author (v0.9.7 in Project.toml, last commit 2026-10-01, MIT, 26 stars, registered in the Julia General registry). It is usable from Julia today, but it has an open GPU out-of-bounds bug for Float32 points just below 0 and weak 2D GPU performance, and the published numbers come from v0.8.3 with tuned σ = 1.5, not the default 2.0.
